opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing is that predictive accuracy is something you can actually check. Right now, when people from different political camps argue about a claim, whether it's about the effects of a minimum wage increase, crime trends, or what a new technology will do, there's often no neutral referee. Each side has its own experts, its own media, and its own reasons to discount the other side's sources. So disputes just persist.

AI systems trained to make accurate forecasts, and scored against what actually happens, change that dynamic in a few ways.

First, you get a track record that doesn't depend on trusting anyone's motives. If a system has made thousands of forecasts about elections, economic indicators, scientific replications, and geopolitical events, and its probabilities turned out well calibrated, that's evidence people across the spectrum can look at. You don't have to believe the developers share your politics. You can look at the scorecard. It's like how prediction markets or superforecasters earn credibility: not through credentials but through being right more often than the alternatives.

Second, these systems can be made to show their work and be tested on whether that reasoning holds up. You can ask: what does this model predict will happen if this policy passes? Then later you can check. And because AI is cheap to run at scale, you can do this for a huge number of claims, far more than human fact-checkers could ever handle.

Third, and I think this is underappreciated, you can design the system so that its outputs are robust to manipulation by any faction. If both sides can audit the training process, see that it was optimized for accuracy rather than for pleasing a particular audience, and run adversarial tests, like checking whether the model gives consistent answers when you flip the political valence of a question, then you build something closer to a common epistemic resource.

Now, there are real challenges. One is that many contested claims are about values, not facts, and a forecasting AI can't settle those. But a surprising amount of political disagreement is actually about empirical predictions dressed up as value disputes. People disagree about whether a policy will reduce poverty or cause unemployment, and those are things you can, at least in principle, forecast and check.

Another challenge is trust in the institutions building these systems. If people suspect a lab has its thumb on the scale, the whole thing falls apart. So you'd want transparency, multiple independent systems that can be compared against each other, and ideally participation from people across the spectrum in setting up evaluation.

But if you get it right, the payoff is large. You could have a situation where, when a politician makes a claim, there's a widely trusted, demonstrably accurate source that can say, "Our best estimate is that this has a 15% chance of being true, and here's our track record on similar claims." That raises the cost of making false claims and gives citizens a way to cut through polarization. As AI becomes more capable, possibly much more capable than human experts at forecasting, that kind of shared standard could become one of the most important tools we have for collective decision-making, including on questions about AI itself.

r002.rationale: It does not explain how bias across many small judgments could accumulate into a radically distorted conclusion.

r003.rationale: It mentions audits and adversarial tests, but not independently applying predictive training and the same interpretability procedures across political factions to produce convergent answers.

r004.rationale: It mentions comparing independent systems, but does not identify agreement among systems built by groups with different allegiances as a signal for observers unable to inspect their reasoning.

r005.rationale: The response discusses institutional trust, but not the difficulty nontechnical bystanders may have distinguishing genuine truth-tracking systems from deceptive ones.

r006.rationale: It does not propose making the reporting of AI conclusions a journalistic norm analogous to accurately reporting sources.

r007.rationale: It says AI is cheap to run at scale, allowing a huge number of claims to be checked—far more than human fact-checkers could handle. That communicates the proposed expansion in scrutiny through lower-cost AI fact-checking.

r008.rationale: It does not explain that independently reproducible assessments could make misrepresentations directly demonstrable, like arithmetic errors in an article.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core idea here is that right now, when people disagree about factual claims — what a policy will do, whether some scientific finding holds up, what's actually happening in a conflict — there's often no neutral arbiter that both sides will accept. If you cite a fact-checker, the other side says the fact-checkers are biased. If you cite experts, well, experts are selected and funded in various ways, and people reasonably suspect motivated reasoning.

What's different about AI trained for predictive accuracy is that you can build in track records that are verifiable in a way that's much harder to dispute. So the model you want to imagine is something like: you have a system that makes probabilistic forecasts about things that will actually resolve — election outcomes, economic indicators, whether a particular bill passes, what a replication study finds. And then you score it. Not on whether its conclusions are congenial to anyone, but on calibration and accuracy against reality. Did the things it said were 90% likely happen about 90% of the time?

And crucially, that scoring can be audited by anyone. Someone on the left and someone on the right can both go look at the resolved predictions and check the math. You don't have to trust the people who built the system. You can verify the outputs. That's a very different epistemic situation than "trust this institution because it has credentials."

Now, the second piece is that once you've established that track record on things that resolve, you've got a basis for extending some credibility to the system's judgments on things that are harder to check directly. If a system has been reliably accurate on thousands of verifiable claims, and it's been trained in a way where lying or spinning would hurt its score, then when it says "this claim about the policy effect is probably false, here's why," that carries weight — and it carries the same weight regardless of your political priors, because the track record was built the same way for everyone.

There's a further thing you can do, which is train systems specifically to make the strongest case for each side and then evaluate those cases, or to predict what a very well-informed person would conclude after seeing all the evidence. So you're not just asking "what's true," you're structuring the process so partisans can see their best arguments were actually represented and engaged with. That matters a lot for buy-in.

I'd also say — this isn't going to make everyone agree on values. Someone can accept that a policy has a particular effect and still disagree about whether that's good. But a huge amount of political disagreement is actually disguised factual disagreement. People argue about immigration or climate or crime as if they're arguing about values, when really they have wildly different beliefs about what's happening in the world. If you could get even partial convergence on the facts, the remaining value disagreements become much more tractable, because you can at least see what trade-offs you're actually arguing about.

The incentive problem is real though. Political actors benefit from being able to make unfalsifiable claims, and they'll resist systems that make those claims checkable. So I don't think this happens automatically. But I do think there's a path where these systems become widely used because they're useful — for investors, for ordinary decision-making, for anyone who actually wants to know what's going to happen — and once they're used for that, their track records become common knowledge, and it becomes socially costly to just dismiss them when they say something you don't like. That's how you'd end up with something closer to a shared standard: not by fiat, but because the systems earn trust in domains where everyone has an interest in being right, and that trust then spills over.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the hope is that predictive accuracy gives you a criterion that cuts across a lot of political disagreements. People can disagree about values, but if they’re making claims about what will happen — what a policy will do to employment, or crime, or health — then those claims have consequences that we can eventually observe.

You could imagine different factions putting forward their own models, and those models being evaluated on the same questions, with predictions recorded in advance. How well calibrated are they? When they say something has an 80% chance of happening, does it happen about 80% of the time? Do they outperform simpler alternatives? That gives you a basis for saying, “This system has earned some credibility,” which doesn’t just amount to, “It agrees with my side.”

And there’s a potentially useful tension there. If you train a system to give politically congenial answers, that can come at the expense of accuracy. If another system consistently makes better predictions, there’s an incentive to use it when you actually care about the outcome. You might prefer reassuring rhetoric in public, but when you’re deciding where to invest resources, you want an accurate picture.

Now, that doesn’t automatically produce agreement. People can contest which questions get asked, how outcomes are measured, and whether success on past questions transfers to a new situation. And some important political disagreements really are about values. But it could give us a shared empirical reference point: a track record that people with quite different commitments can inspect, rather than having every factual dispute turn entirely on which institution they trust.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the basic possibility is that people who disagree quite strongly politically can nevertheless agree on a procedure for testing predictions. You can disagree about what a policy will do, but if you specify the outcome in advance and then observe it, there’s some opportunity to keep score.

With AI, you could have systems trained to make accurate predictions across a very wide range of questions. And you could evaluate those systems prospectively, on events that hadn’t happened when they made their forecasts. So someone might say, “This system gives answers I dislike on some politically charged questions,” but also see that it has a very good track record, including on questions they selected themselves.

That could provide a common reference point. If a politician makes a claim about the consequences of a policy, you could ask what the forecasting systems predict, what evidence would change their predictions, and how well they’ve done on similar questions. And different factions could run their own evaluations and check whether the apparent accuracy holds up.

Now, that doesn’t settle disagreements about values. And it doesn’t automatically make people accept inconvenient facts. There are also problems with choosing the questions, defining outcomes, and extrapolating from things that are easy to score to things that are hard to score. But it could make some factual disagreements more costly to maintain. You’d have an available standard with a demonstrated track record, and people could ask why a particular public claim should be trusted over that.
